A default Rule Set for the thing this project exists to catch: a Test Case that
reads as though a model wrote it. Two tables — one of Terms, one of Symbols —
taken from the published anti-AI-writing work rather than invented here.

Today an operator applying `schema.sql` has an empty `rule_sets` table and a
server that refuses to start. What they write first is guesswork. These two
tables are what they should be able to start from.

## Where these come from

| Source | What was taken |
|---|---|
| [Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing) | Puffery vocabulary, formulaic phrases, negative parallelism, the style/punctuation section |
| [t0ddharris/slopster](https://github.com/t0ddharris/slopster) — Vale lint rules | `BannedWords.yml`, `JargonSwaps.yml`, `WeakWords.yml`, `EmDash.yml`, `AISlop.yml` |
| [jalaalrd/anti-ai-slop-writing](https://github.com/jalaalrd/anti-ai-slop-writing) | `references/banned-words.md` — banned vocabulary, phrases, openers |
| [conorbronsdon/avoid-ai-writing](https://github.com/conorbronsdon/avoid-ai-writing) | Tier 1 / Tier 2 / Tier 3 vocabulary |
| [ama-zingco/anti-ai-writing-skill](https://github.com/ama-zingco/anti-ai-writing-skill) | 25 rules with cited sources (Russell 2025, Economist 2026) |
| [slopdetector.org](https://slopdetector.org/blog/signs-of-ai-writing) | 12 patterns with measured thresholds |

They agree with each other far more than they disagree, which is why one table
can be drawn from all six.

## Table 1 — Terms

A Term Rule matches a word or phrase as written, in any casing, whole. This is
the "simple grep style" half. Every row below is expressible today, with no code
change.

**Inflated vocabulary** — the plain word exists and is shorter.

| Term | Reason the caller is given |
|---|---|
| utilise | Write use. |
| utilize | Write use. |
| leverage | Write use. |
| facilitate | Write help, or name what it does. |
| commence | Write start. |
| demonstrate | Write show. |
| delve | Write examine, or name the step. |
| robust | Name the condition being tested, not its quality. |
| comprehensive | A Test Case covers what it covers. Say what. |
| seamless | Not observable. Name the observable result. |
| streamline | Name the step that is removed. |
| underscore | Write show. |
| showcase | Write show. |
| harness | Write use. |
| bolster | Write strengthen, or name the change. |
| cutting-edge | Marketing, not a test condition. |
| groundbreaking | Marketing, not a test condition. |
| game-changer | Marketing, not a test condition. |
| paradigm | Name the thing itself. |
| holistic | Name what is covered. |
| meticulous | The steps are the detail. Do not claim it. |
| multifaceted | Name the facets or drop the word. |
| nuanced | Name the distinction that matters. |
| transformative | Marketing, not a test condition. |
| pivotal | Name why the step matters, or drop it. |
| crucial | Name why the step matters, or drop it. |
| vital | Name why the step matters, or drop it. |
| testament | Rhetoric. A Test Case states conditions. |
| tapestry | Rhetoric. A Test Case states conditions. |
| landscape | Rhetoric unless it is a literal one. |
| realm | Rhetoric. Name the area. |
| ecosystem | Name the systems involved. |
| empower | Name what the user can now do. |
| elevate | Name the change. |
| unleash | Marketing, not a test condition. |

| Term | Reason the caller is given |
|---|---|

| really | Cut it. |
| extremely | Cut it, or give the number. |

| significantly | Give the number. |
| notably | Cut it. |
| importantly | Cut it. |
| interestingly | Cut it. |

**Openers and transitions** — the shape of generated prose, not of a Test Case.

| Term | Reason the caller is given |

| moreover | Start with the condition. |

| additionally | Start with the condition. |
| in conclusion | A Test Case has no conclusion. |
| at the end of the day | Cut it. |
| in today's | Cut the scene-setting. |
| it's important to note | Cut it and state the thing. |
| it is worth noting | Cut it and state the thing. |
| let's dive in | Cut it. |
| when it comes to | Name the subject directly. |
| in the realm of | Name the area directly. |
| whether you're | Addressing a reader. A Test Case addresses a tester. |

**Contrast frames** — the fixed part of "not X, it's Y". These fire on the

A Symbol Rule matches one character, and `flanked: whitespace` narrows it to
where whitespace sits on both sides. This is the "pattern detect" half, as far
as the engine reaches today.

| Character | Rule | Flanked | Reason the caller is given |
|---|---|---|---|
| `—` em dash | `no-em-dash` | no | The most-cited AI punctuation tell. Use a comma, a colon, or a full stop. |
| `–` en dash | `no-en-dash` | no | Use a hyphen in a range, a full stop otherwise. |
| `-` hyphen | `no-spaced-hyphen` | **yes** | ` - ` is an em dash in disguise. Inside a word it is left alone. |
| `;` semicolon | `no-spaced-semicolon` | **yes** | ` ; ` is spacing no editor produces. |
| `:` colon | `no-spaced-colon` | **yes** | ` : ` is spacing no editor produces. |
| `…` ellipsis | `no-ellipsis` | no | A step either continues or it does not. |
| `"` `"` curly quotes | `no-curly-quote-open` / `-close` | no | Straight quotes only; a Test Case is read by tools. |
| `'` curly apostrophe | `no-curly-apostrophe` | no | Straight apostrophe only. |
| `•` bullet | `no-bullet-character` | no | A field is text, not a rendered list. |
| `→` arrow | `no-arrow` | no | Write the word. |
| `✅` `❌` `⚠` | one Rule each | no | A Test Case carries no decoration. |
| `!` exclamation | `no-exclamation` | no | A Test Case states, it does not exclaim. |

**On ` - `, ` : ` and ` ; ` specifically.** The spaced hyphen is real and well
documented — tools catch `—`, `--` and ` - ` as the same tell. The other two are
not what the research describes, and this is worth knowing before writing them:

- The **colon** tell is a *shape*, not a spaced character: the bolded-header-
  then-colon-then-description bullet, on every item. A spaced ` : ` catches
  almost none of that.
- The **semicolon** tell runs the *other way*. The 2026 measurements say models
  use **fewer** semicolons, commas and parentheses than people do, and that thin
  punctuation is now the stronger signal. A Rule firing on a semicolon would
  penalise the human habit.

Both are in the table because they cost nothing to include and catch odd
spacing. Neither should be believed to be catching an AI tell.

Named so an absent Rule is not read as a clean area. None of these is a defect —
they are the edge of what a Term and a Symbol reach.

| Tell | Why the engine cannot hold it |
|---|---|
| "It's not X — it's Y", "isn't A. It's B" | A Term is literal. The slots are anything. Needs a pattern Rule with holes in it. |
| Rule of three — "efficient, scalable, reliable" | A shape, with no fixed words. |
| Em dashes per 1,000 words | A Rule fires per occurrence; nothing counts. For a Test Case field this is fine — one em dash in a name is one too many — so the threshold rules simply become presence rules. |
| "Punctuate more, not less" | The Rule fires on presence. Absence is not reachable. |
| Uniform sentence length, low burstiness | Statistical over a whole document. |
| Title Case In Headings | Casing is deliberately ignored: a Term matches in any casing. |
| Bold header, colon, description on every bullet | A layout, not a character. |

make roughly six more Rules writable. It is code, tests, README and an ADR, and
nothing here is blocked on it.

ADR-0006 is explicit — the project ships no loader, no write path, nothing. The
server reads and never writes, and that is what keeps the generating agent from
loosening a Rule that keeps rejecting it (ADR-0001). "Default at database" has
to respect that or reverse it.

| Option | What it means | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **A. A SQL file in the repo** | `default-rules.sql`, applied by the operator the way `schema.sql` is. The suite extracts and runs it, so what is documented is what is tested. | Not automatic — the operator chooses to apply it. ADR-0006 untouched. |
| **B. The server seeds on empty** | Truly default; nothing for the operator to do. | Reverses ADR-0006. The server gains a write path into its own Rules. |
| **C. README only** | The tables live as documentation to copy from. | Cheapest. Drifts from what anyone actually runs. |

**A** is the recommendation. **This is the maintainer's call and is not decided
here.**

content.text:
Read all three. Issue 20 is the strongest input here — it's already done the hard part, including the honest boundary.

## What I think

**Your point 2 is the real one.** An agent opening `foo.py` knows the contract; opening `foo.md` it knows nothing — README, test plan, talk track, notes all look identical. And the register isn't just different per kind, **it inverts**. Contractions in a spoken demo script are correct and in a test case are sloppy. "Verify that" is fine in a README and is a finding in a test case — which is exactly what issue 20's QA-specific table encodes. A reviewer that doesn't establish the kind first will apply the wrong sign to half its markers.

So doc-kind isn't a lens among four. It's **step 1**, and it decides what the other steps mean.

**The mechanical half should be a script, not skill text.** Issue 20's two tables are ~60 terms and ~12 symbols, all literal. A model asked to spot its own em dashes returns a confident answer uncorrelated with the text; grep returns the same count every run on every model. And a script costs no context — only its stdout does.

That also imports issue 20's best section, *"What cannot be expressed"*: rule-of-three, the "not X — it's Y" frame with open slots, em-dashes-per-1000-words, uniform sentence length, title case, bold-header-colon layout. Naming those in the skill is what stops a clean script run reading as a clean document.

## One skill, not two

Split and you get two units that must always run together — which is the CUT condition in `reviewing-artifacts`, and nothing would say which one ran. The sequence is **grep → judge**, not two reviews:

```
1. IDENTIFY   what is this file, who reads it, what register does that kind take
2. RUN        check-prose.sh  →  located candidates, counted
3. JUDGE      did each hit cost this reader — and the shapes grep cannot reach
```

The script goes beside `SKILL.md`, not under it — `skills/reviewing-phrasing/check-prose.sh` — per the flat-skills rule.

## The kinds I'd name

| Kind | Reader is | Register |
|---|---|---|
| README | a newcomer scanning | leads with the point, second person fine |
| Test plan / case | a tester executing | imperative, precise; quality adjectives are findings |
| Design doc / RFC | a peer deciding | the argument must be followable, so prose earns its length |
| Release notes | someone asking "does this affect me" | terse, changes first |
| Talk track / demo script | **listened to** | contractions right, long clauses wrong, em dashes invisible |
| Slide content | read in 3 seconds while someone talks | fragments right, sentences wrong |
| Reference / API | looked up, not read | consistency beats flow |

## One thing to settle first

You have `.claude/skills/writing-technical-docs/` with reference files for exactly `test-plans`, `readmes`, `api-reference`, `design-docs`. That's the authoring counterpart, and it already holds doc-kind knowledge. Same shape as `writing-agent-skills`: local standard, shipped reviewer.

If the reviewer restates those kinds, they drift. If it defers, it breaks downstream where that skill doesn't exist. My call is the reviewer carries only what changes a *verdict* — reader and register per kind, one line each — and leaves structure and content to the authoring skill.

Go?

1	---
2	name: writing-technical-docs
3	description: Write and review technical documentation in English — design docs, RFCs, READMEs, test plans, QA reports, and API or tool reference docs. Covers audience calibration, document structure, precise sentence-level style, code examples, tables and diagrams, and review checklists per document type. Use whenever the user is drafting, restructuring, editing, or critiquing any technical document, writing up a design or proposal, documenting a repository or tool, reporting test results, or asking how a document should be organized — including phrasings like "write this up", "document this", "does this read okay", or "make this clearer" that never say the word documentation.
4	---
5	
6	# Writing Technical Docs
7	
8	Principles and patterns for technical prose in English. Universal rules live here; per-document-type structure lives in `reference/`.
9	
10	## Route by document type
11	
12	| Writing | Read |
13	|---|---|
14	| Design doc, RFC, ADR, proposal | [reference/design-docs.md](reference/design-docs.md) |
15	| README, contributing guide, project docs | [reference/readmes.md](reference/readmes.md) |
16	| Test plan, test strategy, QA report, bug report | [reference/test-plans.md](reference/test-plans.md) |
17	| API reference, CLI docs, MCP tool docs, schema docs | [reference/api-reference.md](reference/api-reference.md) |
18	
19	Read the matching file before drafting. The universal principles below apply to all four.
20	
21	## Establish the reader before the outline
22	
23	Every structural decision follows from three answers. If they aren't inferable from the request, ask:
24	
25	1. **Who reads this, and what do they already know?** A reviewer on the same team needs no background section. An external contributor needs one.
26	2. **What decision or action does the document enable?** Approving a design, running a build, filing a bug, calling an endpoint. A document that enables nothing should not exist.
27	3. **How will it be read?** Start to finish (design docs, reports), or jumped into via search and skim (READMEs, reference docs). Skimmed documents need aggressive headings and self-contained sections.
28	
29	Write for the least informed reader who must act on it, not for the author's future self.
30	
31	## Front-load
32	
33	Readers stop early. Put the conclusion, the recommendation, or the working command in the first screen; put derivation and detail below.
34	
35	Bad:
36	
37	> We evaluated three approaches. Approach A was considered first, which involved... Approach B... After extensive analysis, we recommend Approach C.
38	
39	Good:
40	
41	> **Recommendation: Approach C.** It is the only option that preserves existing test IDs during migration. Approaches A and B are compared below.
42	
43	This applies fractally — the first sentence of every section states its point, and the rest supports it.
44	
45	## Structure
46	
47	- One idea per section, one point per paragraph, one action per step.
48	- Headings are informative, not cute: "Handling partial writes", not "The tricky part".
49	- Prefer four to seven top-level sections. More means the document is really two documents.
50	- Numbered lists for ordered procedures; bullets for unordered sets; tables for anything with more than two parallel attributes.
51	- If a paragraph contains three or more parallel comparisons, it wants to be a table.
52	
53	## Sentence-level style
54	
55	**Present tense, active voice, indicative mood.** "The validator rejects the field" — not "the field will be rejected by the validator".
56	
57	**Imperative for instructions.** "Run the migration" — not "you should run the migration" or "we can now run the migration".
58	
59	**Delete hedges and filler.** *simply, just, basically, obviously, of course, note that, it should be noted that, in order to, at this point in time.* If something is obvious, saying so insults readers who find it isn't.
60	
61	**One term per concept, forever.** Choosing `test case` means never writing `test`, `case`, or `TC` for the same thing. Synonym variation is a virtue in prose and a defect in technical writing — the reader must decide whether a new word means a new thing.
62	
63	**Quantify.** "Slow" → "roughly 4s per 1000 records". "Large" → "over 50 MB". "Frequently" → "on every write".
64	
65	**No dangling pronouns.** "This causes failures" — *this* what? Name the referent: "This retry loop causes failures".
66	
67	**Split sentences carrying more than one clause of new information.** A sentence with three commas is usually three sentences.
68	
69	**Second person for the reader, never first person plural for the reader's actions.** "You configure the endpoint" — not "we configure the endpoint", unless describing what the authoring team itself did.
70	
71	## Code and commands
72	
73	- Every example must run as written. Copy it, execute it, then paste it back.
74	- Show the invocation *and* a representative output; readers verify against output.
75	- Use realistic values, not `foo`/`bar`. `--project TestLink-QA` teaches more than `--project myproject`.
76	- Mark placeholders unmistakably: `<your-api-token>`, not `YOUR_API_TOKEN` mixed among real flags.
77	- Never prefix shell lines with `$` when the block is meant to be copied — it breaks paste.
78	- Include the failure path when it is likely: what the error looks like, what it means, what to do.
79	- Specify versions when behavior depends on them; omit them when it doesn't, since stale versions erode trust in the whole page.
80	
81	## Tables and diagrams
82	
83	Tables need a stable column set — same attributes, same order, for every row. If a row needs "N/A" in half its cells, it doesn't belong in that table.
84	
85	Use a diagram when the relationship is spatial or topological (component boundaries, data flow, state transitions, sequence across processes). Do not use one to restate a list. Every diagram needs a caption stating what the reader should conclude from it — an uncaptioned diagram is decoration.
86	
87	Prefer text-source diagrams (Mermaid, Graphviz) that live in version control beside the doc over exported images that rot.
88	
89	## Resisting rot
90	
91	- No relative time: "currently", "recently", "the new API", "as of this quarter". Write the condition instead: "in v2.3 and later".
92	- No links to internal chat threads or ticket comments as the sole source of a decision — restate the decision in the document.
93	- Deprecated material goes in a clearly marked section at the bottom, not deleted (readers still hit old versions) and not inline (it competes with current guidance).
94	- State the document's status explicitly if it can go stale: draft, accepted, superseded by X.
95	
96	## Review pass
97	
98	Run this on any draft, yours or someone else's:
99	
100	```
101	- [ ] First screen states the conclusion or the working example
102	- [ ] Reader and their prior knowledge are identifiable from the text
103	- [ ] Every section heading predicts its content
104	- [ ] One term per concept, checked by searching for synonyms
105	- [ ] All code examples executed as written
106	- [ ] Vague quantifiers replaced with numbers
107	- [ ] No hedges, no "simply", no "just"
108	- [ ] Tables have uniform columns; diagrams have captions
109	- [ ] No relative time references
110	- [ ] Cut 20% — every remaining sentence earns its place
111	```
112	
113	The last item is not rhetorical. First drafts are reliably 20% longer than their final form, and the cut almost always improves them.
114	
115	## Reviewing someone else's draft
116	
117	Separate the levels and lead with the highest one — structural problems make sentence edits wasted work.
118	
119	1. **Does it serve its purpose?** Wrong audience, missing decision, or a document that shouldn't exist.
120	2. **Is the structure right?** Missing sections, wrong order, buried conclusion.
121	3. **Is it accurate?** Broken examples, stale versions, unsupported claims.
122	4. **Is the prose clean?** Voice, terminology, hedging.
123	
124	Give the author the reasoning, not just the correction: "moved the recommendation up — reviewers approving this won't read past the first screen" rather than a silent reordering.

| API reference, CLI docs, MCP tool docs, schema docs | [reference/api-reference.md](reference/api-reference.md) |

Read the matching file before drafting. The universal principles below apply to all four.

## Establish the reader before the outline

Every structural decision follows from three answers. If they aren't inferable from the request, ask:

1. **Who reads this, and what do they already know?** A reviewer on the same team needs no background section. An external contributor needs one.
2. **What decision or action does the document enable?** Approving a design, running a build, filing a bug, calling an endpoint. A document that enables nothing should not exist.
3. **How will it be read?** Start to finish (design docs, reports), or jumped into via search and skim (READMEs, reference docs). Skimmed documents need aggressive headings and self-contained sections.

Write for the least informed reader who must act on it, not for the author's future self.

## Front-load

Readers stop early. Put the conclusion, the recommendation, or the working command in the first screen; put derivation and detail below.

Bad:

> We evaluated three approaches. Approach A was considered first, which involved... Approach B... After extensive analysis, we recommend Approach C.

Good:

> **Recommendation: Approach C.** It is the only option that preserves existing test IDs during migration. Approaches A and B are compared below.

This applies fractally — the first sentence of every section states its point, and the rest supports it.

## Structure

- One idea per section, one point per paragraph, one action per step.
- Headings are informative, not cute: "Handling partial writes", not "The tricky part".
- Prefer four to seven top-level sections. More means the document is really two documents.
- Numbered lists for ordered procedures; bullets for unordered sets; tables for anything with more than two parallel attributes.
- If a paragraph contains three or more parallel comparisons, it wants to be a table.

## Sentence-level style

**Present tense, active voice, indicative mood.** "The validator rejects the field" — not "the field will be rejected by the validator".

**Imperative for instructions.** "Run the migration" — not "you should run the migration" or "we can now run the migration".

**Delete hedges and filler.** *simply, just, basically, obviously, of course, note that, it should be noted that, in order to, at this point in time.* If something is obvious, saying so insults readers who find it isn't.

**One term per concept, forever.** Choosing `test case` means never writing `test`, `case`, or `TC` for the same thing. Synonym variation is a virtue in prose and a defect in technical writing — the reader must decide whether a new word means a new thing.

**Quantify.** "Slow" → "roughly 4s per 1000 records". "Large" → "over 50 MB". "Frequently" → "on every write".

**No dangling pronouns.** "This causes failures" — *this* what? Name the referent: "This retry loop causes failures".

**Split sentences carrying more than one clause of new information.** A sentence with three commas is usually three sentences.

**Second person for the reader, never first person plural for the reader's actions.** "You configure the endpoint" — not "we configure the endpoint", unless describing what the authoring team itself did.

## Code and commands

- Every example must run as written. Copy it, execute it, then paste it back.
- Show the invocation *and* a representative output; readers verify against output.
- Use realistic values, not `foo`/`bar`. `--project TestLink-QA` teaches more than `--project myproject`.
- Mark placeholders unmistakably: `<your-api-token>`, not `YOUR_API_TOKEN` mixed among real flags.
- Never prefix shell lines with `$` when the block is meant to be copied — it breaks paste.
- Include the failure path when it is likely: what the error looks like, what it means, what to do.
- Specify versions when behavior depends on them; omit them when it doesn't, since stale versions erode trust in the whole page.

## Tables and diagrams

Tables need a stable column set — same attributes, same order, for every row. If a row needs "N/A" in half its cells, it doesn't belong in that table.

Use a diagram when the relationship is spatial or topological (component boundaries, data flow, state transitions, sequence across processes). Do not use one to restate a list. Every diagram needs a caption stating what the reader should conclude from it — an uncaptioned diagram is decoration.

Prefer text-source diagrams (Mermaid, Graphviz) that live in version control beside the doc over exported images that rot.

## Resisting rot

- No relative time: "currently", "recently", "the new API", "as of this quarter". Write the condition instead: "in v2.3 and later".
- No links to internal chat threads or ticket comments as the sole source of a decision — restate the decision in the document.
- Deprecated material goes in a clearly marked section at the bottom, not deleted (readers still hit old versions) and not inline (it competes with current guidance).
- State the document's status explicitly if it can go stale: draft, accepted, superseded by X.

## Review pass

Run this on any draft, yours or someone else's:

```
- [ ] First screen states the conclusion or the working example
- [ ] Reader and their prior knowledge are identifiable from the text
- [ ] Every section heading predicts its content
- [ ] One term per concept, checked by searching for synonyms
- [ ] All code examples executed as written
- [ ] Vague quantifiers replaced with numbers
- [ ] No hedges, no "simply", no "just"
- [ ] Tables have uniform columns; diagrams have captions
- [ ] No relative time references
- [ ] Cut 20% — every remaining sentence earns its place
```

The last item is not rhetorical. First drafts are reliably 20% longer than their final form, and the cut almost always improves them.

## Reviewing someone else's draft

Separate the levels and lead with the highest one — structural problems make sentence edits wasted work.

1. **Does it serve its purpose?** Wrong audience, missing decision, or a document that shouldn't exist.
2. **Is the structure right?** Missing sections, wrong order, buried conclusion.
3. **Is it accurate?** Broken examples, stale versions, unsupported claims.
4. **Is the prose clean?** Voice, terminology, hedging.

Give the author the reasoning, not just the correction: "moved the recommendation up — reviewers approving this won't read past the first screen" rather than a silent reordering.

#!/bin/sh
# Locate the mechanical AI-writing tells in a document.
#
# These are CANDIDATES, not findings. A hit costs the reader or it does not,
# and only judgment decides which — see SKILL.md. What this buys is that the
# searching stops depending on the model's mood: the same file gives the same
# counts on every run, on every model.
#
# Exits 0 even with hits, deliberately. It locates; it does not grade.
#
# Usage:  check-prose.sh <file>...

set -u
[ $# -eq 0 ] && { echo "usage: check-prose.sh <file>..." >&2; exit 2; }

for F in "$@"; do
  [ -f "$F" ] || { echo "no such file: $F" >&2; continue; }
  echo "══ $F"

  # ---- symbols: one character, exact ------------------------------------
  # Straight from the symbol table. Each is a character an editor does not
  # produce by accident.
  echo "-- symbols"
  sym() { n=$(grep -c "$1" "$F" 2>/dev/null || echo 0); [ "$n" -gt 0 ] && printf '  %-22s %3d   %s\n' "$2" "$n" "$3"; }
  sym '—'        'em dash'          'the most-cited tell — comma, colon, or full stop'
  sym '–'        'en dash'          'hyphen in a range, full stop otherwise'
  sym ' - '      'spaced hyphen'    'an em dash in disguise'
  sym '…'        'ellipsis'         'it continues or it does not'
  sym '“\|”'     'curly quote'      'straight quotes only'
  sym '’'        'curly apostrophe' 'straight apostrophe only'
  sym '•'        'bullet char'      'use a real list'
  sym '→'        'arrow'            'write the word'
  sym '!'        'exclamation'      'technical prose states, it does not exclaim'
  grep -nP '[\x{1F300}-\x{1FAFF}\x{2600}-\x{27BF}\x{2705}\x{274C}\x{26A0}]' "$F" 2>/dev/null \
    | head -5 | sed 's/^/  emoji  /'

  # ---- em dash as a RATE, which presence alone cannot show --------------
  words=$(wc -w < "$F")
  dashes=$(grep -o '—' "$F" 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
  [ "$words" -gt 0 ] && [ "$dashes" -gt 0 ] && \
    printf '  %-22s %3d per 1000 words\n' 'em-dash rate' $(( dashes * 1000 / words ))

  # ---- terms: literal, any casing, whole word ---------------------------
  echo "-- terms"
  term() {
    hits=$(grep -inoE "\\b($1)\\b" "$F" 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
    [ "$hits" -gt 0 ] && printf '  %-14s %3d   %s\n' "$2" "$hits" "$3"
  }
  # inflated: the plain word exists and is shorter
  term 'utilise|utilize|leverage|harness' 'inflated:use'    'write use'
  term 'facilitate'                       'inflated'        'write help, or name what it does'
  term 'commence'                         'inflated'        'write start'
  term 'demonstrate|showcase|underscore'  'inflated:show'   'write show'
  term 'delve'                            'inflated'        'write examine, or name the step'
  term 'robust|comprehensive|holistic'    'inflated:claim'  'name what is covered, not its quality'
  term 'seamless|seamlessly|streamline'   'inflated'        'name the observable result'
  term 'cutting-edge|groundbreaking|game-changer|transformative|unleash' 'marketing' 'not a technical claim'
  term 'paradigm|tapestry|realm|landscape|testament|ecosystem' 'rhetoric' 'name the thing itself'
  term 'meticulous|multifaceted|nuanced'  'inflated'        'name the detail or drop it'
  term 'pivotal|crucial|vital'            'inflated'        'name why it matters, or drop it'
  term 'empower|elevate|bolster'          'inflated'        'name the change'
  # filler: carries nothing
  term 'very|really|extremely|incredibly' 'filler'          'cut it, or give the number'
  term 'basically|essentially|simply|just' 'filler'         'cut it'
  term 'clearly|obviously'                'filler'          'if it is, it needs no saying'
  term 'significantly|notably|importantly|interestingly' 'filler' 'give the number, or cut'
  # openers and transitions: the shape of generated prose
  term 'moreover|furthermore|additionally' 'opener'         'start with the point'
  term 'in conclusion|at the end of the day' 'opener'       'cut it'
  term "it'?s important to note|it is worth noting|let'?s dive in" 'opener' 'cut it and state the thing'
  term "in today'?s|when it comes to|in the realm of" 'opener' 'name the subject directly'
  # contrast frames: the fixed half of "not X, it's Y"
  term "not just|not only|here'?s the thing|this is where" 'contrast-frame' 'state what it is'
  # hedges
  term 'arguably|generally|typically|somewhat|relatively|fairly' 'hedge' 'state the claim, or name what it varies with'
  term 'may help|can often|might potentially' 'hedge'       'state the claim'
  # technical-document specific: a quality adjective standing in for a result
  term 'successfully|properly|correctly|as expected' 'unobservable' 'name the observable result'
  term 'appropriate|various|etc'          'vague'           'name it, or give the count'
  term 'verify that|ensure that'          'qa-filler'       'name what is checked, not that it is checked'
  # rot: relative time goes stale on its own
  term 'currently|recently|nowadays|at this time' 'relative-time' 'write the condition, e.g. "in v2.3 and later"'

  echo
done
exit 0

# Usage:  check-prose.sh <file>...

set -u
[ $# -eq 0 ] && { echo "usage: check-prose.sh <file>..." >&2; exit 2; }

for F in "$@"; do
  [ -f "$F" ] || { echo "no such file: $F" >&2; continue; }
  echo "══ $F"

  # ---- symbols: one character, exact ------------------------------------
  # Straight from the symbol table. Each is a character an editor does not
  # produce by accident.
  echo "-- symbols"
  sym() { n=$(grep -c "$1" "$F" 2>/dev/null || echo 0); [ "$n" -gt 0 ] && printf '  %-22s %3d   %s\n' "$2" "$n" "$3"; }
  sym '—'        'em dash'          'the most-cited tell — comma, colon, or full stop'
  sym '–'        'en dash'          'hyphen in a range, full stop otherwise'
  sym ' - '      'spaced hyphen'    'an em dash in disguise'
  sym '…'        'ellipsis'         'it continues or it does not'
  sym '“\|”'     'curly quote'      'straight quotes only'
  sym '’'        'curly apostrophe' 'straight apostrophe only'
  sym '•'        'bullet char'      'use a real list'
  sym '→'        'arrow'            'write the word'
  sym '!'        'exclamation'      'technical prose states, it does not exclaim'
  grep -nP '[\x{1F300}-\x{1FAFF}\x{2600}-\x{27BF}\x{2705}\x{274C}\x{26A0}]' "$F" 2>/dev/null \
    | head -5 | sed 's/^/  emoji  /'

  # ---- em dash as a RATE, which presence alone cannot show --------------
  words=$(wc -w < "$F")
  dashes=$(grep -o '—' "$F" 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
  [ "$words" -gt 0 ] && [ "$dashes" -gt 0 ] && \
    printf '  %-22s %3d per 1000 words\n' 'em-dash rate' $(( dashes * 1000 / words ))

  # ---- terms: literal, any casing, whole word ---------------------------
  echo "-- terms"
  term() {
    hits=$(grep -inoE "\\b($1)\\b" "$F" 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
    [ "$hits" -gt 0 ] && printf '  %-14s %3d   %s\n' "$2" "$hits" "$3"
  }

  term 'utilise|utilize|leverage|harness' 'inflated:use'    'write use'
  term 'facilitate'                       'inflated'        'write help, or name what it does'
  term 'commence'                         'inflated'        'write start'
  term 'demonstrate|showcase|underscore'  'inflated:show'   'write show'
  term 'delve'                            'inflated'        'write examine, or name the step'
  term 'robust|comprehensive|holistic'    'inflated:claim'  'name what is covered, not its quality'
  term 'seamless|seamlessly|streamline'   'inflated'        'name the observable result'
  term 'cutting-edge|groundbreaking|game-changer|transformative|unleash' 'marketing' 'not a technical claim'
  term 'paradigm|tapestry|realm|landscape|testament|ecosystem' 'rhetoric' 'name the thing itself'
  term 'meticulous|multifaceted|nuanced'  'inflated'        'name the detail or drop it'
  term 'pivotal|crucial|vital'            'inflated'        'name why it matters, or drop it'
  term 'empower|elevate|bolster'          'inflated'        'name the change'
  # filler: carries nothing
  term 'very|really|extremely|incredibly' 'filler'          'cut it, or give the number'
  term 'basically|essentially|simply|just' 'filler'         'cut it'
  term 'clearly|obviously'                'filler'          'if it is, it needs no saying'
  term 'significantly|notably|importantly|interestingly' 'filler' 'give the number, or cut'
  # openers and transitions: the shape of generated prose
  term 'moreover|furthermore|additionally' 'opener'         'start with the point'
  term 'in conclusion|at the end of the day' 'opener'       'cut it'
  term "it'?s important to note|it is worth noting|let'?s dive in" 'opener' 'cut it and state the thing'
  term "in today'?s|when it comes to|in the realm of" 'opener' 'name the subject directly'
  # contrast frames: the fixed half of "not X, it's Y"
  term "not just|not only|here'?s the thing|this is where" 'contrast-frame' 'state what it is'
  # hedges
  term 'arguably|generally|typically|somewhat|relatively|fairly' 'hedge' 'state the claim, or name what it varies with'
  term 'may help|can often|might potentially' 'hedge'       'state the claim'
  # technical-document specific: a quality adjective standing in for a result
  term 'successfully|properly|correctly|as expected' 'unobservable' 'name the observable result'
  term 'appropriate|various|etc'          'vague'           'name it, or give the count'
  term 'verify that|ensure that'          'qa-filler'       'name what is checked, not that it is checked'
  # rot: relative time goes stale on its own
  term 'currently|recently|nowadays|at this time' 'relative-time' 'write the condition, e.g. "in v2.3 and later"'

---
name: reviewing-phrasing
description: |
  Reviews the words of a document a person will read, and returns PASS or REVISE. Starts
  by establishing what the file actually is and who reads it, because a markdown file
  carries no contract the way a source file does, and the same wording is correct in a
  talk track and wrong in a test case. Then runs check-prose.sh to locate the mechanical
  tells by grep rather than by impression, and judges what a pattern cannot reach.
when_to_use: |
  Use whenever prose a person will read is written or edited: a README, a design doc or
  RFC, a test plan, a QA report, a bug report, API or CLI reference, release notes, slide
  content, a demo script. Also on request: "does this read okay", "make this clearer",
  "tighten this up", "write this up", "too wordy". Reach for it on a document that is
  factually correct and still hard to read, and on any document an agent generated, which
  is the case that most needs it and least asks for it.
argument-hint: "[doc-path]"
---

# Reviewing phrasing

**An agent knows what a `.py` file is and does not know what a `.md` file is.** A source
file declares its contract: imports, signatures, types. A text file declares nothing. A
README, a test case, a talk track and a page of notes are the same bytes to a reader that
has not asked what it is holding.

That matters because the markers invert. Contractions are right in something spoken and
sloppy in a test case. "Verify that" is unremarkable in a README and a finding in a test
step. A reviewer that skips step 1 applies half its rules with the sign flipped.

## 1. Identify the document

Three questions, answered before reading for style. Ask if the file does not say.

1. **Who reads this, and what do they already know?** A teammate needs no background
   section; an external contributor does. Write for the least informed reader who must act
   on it.
2. **What decision or action does it enable?** Approving a design, running a build, filing
   a bug, executing a test, calling an endpoint. A document that enables nothing should not
   exist, and that is a finding on its own.
3. **How is it read?** Start to finish, jumped into by search, or listened to. A skimmed
   document needs headings that predict their content; a spoken one needs none at all.

| Kind | Reader is | Register that is correct here |
|---|---|---|
| README | a newcomer scanning | leads with the point; second person; imperative |
| Design doc / RFC / ADR | a peer deciding | prose earns its length; the argument must follow |
| Test plan / test case | a tester executing | imperative, precise; quality adjectives are findings |
| QA report | someone making a release call | verdict first with its condition; counts, not adjectives |
| Bug report | whoever reproduces it | the reproducer is the document; verbatim error text |
| API / CLI reference | someone looking one thing up | consistency beats flow; every example runs |
| Release notes | someone asking "does this affect me" | changes first, terse |
| Slide content | read in three seconds while someone talks | fragments right, sentences wrong |
| Talk track / demo script | **listened to** | contractions right, long clauses wrong, punctuation invisible |

Four kinds have their own criteria, including per-kind review checklists. Read the matching
file before judging:

| Reviewing | Read |
|---|---|
| Design doc, RFC, ADR, proposal | [reference/design-docs.md](reference/design-docs.md) |
| README, contributing guide, project docs | [reference/readmes.md](reference/readmes.md) |
| Test plan, test case, QA report, bug report | [reference/test-plans.md](reference/test-plans.md) |
| API reference, CLI docs, tool docs, schema docs | [reference/api-reference.md](reference/api-reference.md) |

## 2. Run the script

    ./check-prose.sh <file>

It locates the mechanical tells: the symbol set (em dash, en dash, spaced hyphen, curly
quotes, ellipsis, arrows, emoji), the em-dash rate per thousand words, and the term tables
for inflated vocabulary, filler, openers, contrast frames, hedges, unobservable quality
words and relative time.

**A hit is a located candidate, not a finding.** The script does the searching, which a
model does unreliably on its own writing, and leaves the ruling to step 3. It exits 0 with
hits for exactly that reason. Hedging where a fact is genuinely uncertain is the word doing
its job.

**Run it, do not reimplement it.** Judging your own register is the one thing a generator
is worst at, because fluent-and-empty is its own baseline.

### What the script cannot reach

Named so a clean run is never read as a clean document:

- **The full contrast frame.** It catches `not just` and `not only`; the shape
  "it isn't A, it's B" has open slots and needs a reader.
- **Rule of three.** Matched triads carrying one idea have no fixed words.
- **Restatement.** The next sentence saying the last one again.
- **Vagueness.** A claim with no number, name or path in it, that no pattern marks.
- **Uniform sentence length**, and prose chopped into bullets.
- **Whether a hedge is earned**, which is the whole judgment.

## 3. Judge

**Lead with the highest level.** Structural problems make sentence edits wasted work, so
settle them first:

1. **Does it serve its purpose?** Wrong reader, missing decision, a document that should
   not exist.
2. **Is the structure right?** Missing sections, wrong order, buried conclusion.
3. **Is it accurate?** Broken examples, stale versions, unsupported claims.
4. **Is the prose clean?** Voice, terminology, hedging.

**Front-load.** Readers stop early. The conclusion, the recommendation, or the working
command belongs on the first screen. This applies fractally: the first sentence of every
section states its point.

**The sentence rules**, each a finding when broken:

- Present tense, active voice. "The validator rejects the field", not "the field will be
  rejected".
- Imperative for instructions. "Run the migration", not "you should run the migration".
- One term per concept, forever. Choosing `test case` means never writing `test`, `case` or
  `TC` for it. Synonym variation is a virtue in prose and a defect in technical writing:
  the reader has to decide whether a new word means a new thing.
- Quantify. "Slow" becomes "roughly 4s per 1000 records"; "large" becomes "over 50 MB".
- No dangling pronouns. "This causes failures" — this what? Name the referent.
- Split a sentence carrying more than one clause of new information. Three commas is
  usually three sentences.
- Second person for the reader's actions, not first person plural.
- No relative time. "Currently", "recently", "the new API" rot on their own. Write the
  condition: "in v2.3 and later".

**Cut 20%.** Not rhetorical. First drafts run reliably long, and the cut almost always
improves them.

**Give the reasoning with the correction.** "Moved the recommendation up, because a
reviewer approving this will not read past the first screen" teaches; a silent reordering
does not.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Kind, reader and register established
    - [ ] Matching reference/ file read, if one applies
    - [ ] check-prose.sh run, output kept
    - [ ] Each hit ruled on — cost the reader, or not
    - [ ] The shapes the script cannot reach, judged by reading
    - [ ] Verdict reported

1. **Identify** (step 1). If the kind is genuinely unclear, ask rather than guess.
2. **Run the script** (step 2).
3. **Judge** (step 3), highest level first, whole document.
4. **Report** (below).
5. **Fix, if asked.** The smallest change that lands the words, in the author's voice.
   Leave what already works.

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    REVISE — reads as a design doc but the recommendation is on screen three.
    Next: move the recommendation up, then re-run the script.
    Run it, or see the findings?

- **PASS** — fits its reader, leads with the point, says the true thing.
- **REVISE** — findings, each quoting the words at fault and naming the smallest fix.

Findings, the script output, and the trace are prepared and held until asked. When findings
are given, quote the text rather than describing it, and say which came from the script and
which from reading: a count is reproducible and a judgment is not, and the reader is
entitled to know which they are being handed.

| API / CLI reference | someone looking one thing up | consistency beats flow; every example runs |
| Release notes | someone asking "does this affect me" | changes first, terse |
| Slide content | read in three seconds while someone talks | fragments right, sentences wrong |
| Talk track / demo script | **listened to** | contractions right, long clauses wrong, punctuation invisible |

file before judging:

| Reviewing | Read |
|---|---|
| Design doc, RFC, ADR, proposal | [reference/design-docs.md](reference/design-docs.md) |
| README, contributing guide, project docs | [reference/readmes.md](reference/readmes.md) |
| Test plan, test case, QA report, bug report | [reference/test-plans.md](reference/test-plans.md) |
| API reference, CLI docs, tool docs, schema docs | [reference/api-reference.md](reference/api-reference.md) |

## 2. Run the script

    ./check-prose.sh <file>

It locates the mechanical tells: the symbol set (em dash, en dash, spaced hyphen, curly
quotes, ellipsis, arrows, emoji), the em-dash rate per thousand words, and the term tables
for inflated vocabulary, filler, openers, contrast frames, hedges, unobservable quality
words and relative time.

**A hit is a located candidate, not a finding.** The script does the searching, which a
model does unreliably on its own writing, and leaves the ruling to step 3. It exits 0 with
hits for exactly that reason. Hedging where a fact is genuinely uncertain is the word doing
its job.

**Run it, do not reimplement it.** Judging your own register is the one thing a generator
is worst at, because fluent-and-empty is its own baseline.

### What the script cannot reach

Named so a clean run is never read as a clean document:

- **The full contrast frame.** It catches `not just` and `not only`; the shape
  "it isn't A, it's B" has open slots and needs a reader.
- **Rule of three.** Matched triads carrying one idea have no fixed words.
- **Restatement.** The next sentence saying the last one again.
- **Vagueness.** A claim with no number, name or path in it, that no pattern marks.
- **Uniform sentence length**, and prose chopped into bullets.
- **Whether a hedge is earned**, which is the whole judgment.

## 3. Judge

**Lead with the highest level.** Structural problems make sentence edits wasted work, so
settle them first:

1. **Does it serve its purpose?** Wrong reader, missing decision, a document that should
   not exist.
2. **Is the structure right?** Missing sections, wrong order, buried conclusion.
3. **Is it accurate?** Broken examples, stale versions, unsupported claims.
4. **Is the prose clean?** Voice, terminology, hedging.

**Front-load.** Readers stop early. The conclusion, the recommendation, or the working
command belongs on the first screen. This applies fractally: the first sentence of every
section states its point.

**The sentence rules**, each a finding when broken:

- Present tense, active voice. "The validator rejects the field", not "the field will be
  rejected".
- Imperative for instructions. "Run the migration", not "you should run the migration".
- One term per concept, forever. Choosing `test case` means never writing `test`, `case` or
  `TC` for it. Synonym variation is a virtue in prose and a defect in technical writing:
  the reader has to decide whether a new word means a new thing.
- Quantify. "Slow" becomes "roughly 4s per 1000 records"; "large" becomes "over 50 MB".
- No dangling pronouns. "This causes failures" — this what? Name the referent.
- Split a sentence carrying more than one clause of new information. Three commas is
  usually three sentences.
- Second person for the reader's actions, not first person plural.
- No relative time. "Currently", "recently", "the new API" rot on their own. Write the
  condition: "in v2.3 and later".

**Cut 20%.** Not rhetorical. First drafts run reliably long, and the cut almost always
improves them.

**Give the reasoning with the correction.** "Moved the recommendation up, because a
reviewer approving this will not read past the first screen" teaches; a silent reordering
does not.

    - [ ] Kind, reader and register established

    - [ ] check-prose.sh run, output kept
    - [ ] Each hit ruled on — cost the reader, or not
    - [ ] The shapes the script cannot reach, judged by reading
    - [ ] Verdict reported

1. **Identify** (step 1). If the kind is genuinely unclear, ask rather than guess.
2. **Run the script** (step 2).
3. **Judge** (step 3), highest level first, whole document.
4. **Report** (below).
5. **Fix, if asked.** The smallest change that lands the words, in the author's voice.
   Leave what already works.

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    REVISE — reads as a design doc but the recommendation is on screen three.
    Next: move the recommendation up, then re-run the script.
    Run it, or see the findings?

- **PASS** — fits its reader, leads with the point, says the true thing.
- **REVISE** — findings, each quoting the words at fault and naming the smallest fix.

are given, quote the text rather than describing it, and say which came from the script and
which from reading: a count is reproducible and a judgment is not, and the reader is
entitled to know which they are being handed.

---
name: reviewing-phrasing
description: |
  Reviews the words of a document a person will read, and returns PASS or REVISE. Starts
  by establishing what the file actually is and who reads it, because a markdown file
  carries no contract the way a source file does, and the same wording is correct in a
  talk track and wrong in a test case. Then runs check-prose.sh to locate the mechanical
  tells by grep rather than by impression, and judges what a pattern cannot reach.
when_to_use: |
  Use whenever prose a person will read is written or edited: a README, a design doc or
  RFC, a test plan, a QA report, a bug report, API or CLI reference, release notes, slide
  content, a demo script. Also on request: "does this read okay", "make this clearer",
  "tighten this up", "write this up", "too wordy". Reach for it on a document that is
  factually correct and still hard to read, and on any document an agent generated, which
  is the case that most needs it and least asks for it.
argument-hint: "[doc-path]"
---

# Reviewing phrasing

**An agent knows what a `.py` file is and does not know what a `.md` file is.** A source
file declares its contract: imports, signatures, types. A text file declares nothing. A
README, a test case, a talk track and a page of notes are the same bytes to a reader that
has not asked what it is holding.

That matters because the markers invert. Contractions are right in something spoken and
sloppy in a test case. "Verify that" is unremarkable in a README and a finding in a test
step. A reviewer that skips step 1 applies half its rules with the sign flipped.

## 1. Identify the document

Three questions, answered before reading for style. Ask if the file does not say.

1. **Who reads this, and what do they already know?** A teammate needs no background
   section; an external contributor does. Write for the least informed reader who must act
   on it.
2. **What decision or action does it enable?** Approving a design, running a build, filing
   a bug, executing a test, calling an endpoint. A document that enables nothing should not
   exist, and that is a finding on its own.
3. **How is it read?** Start to finish, jumped into by search, or listened to. A skimmed
   document needs headings that predict their content; a spoken one needs none at all.

| Kind | Reader is | Register that is correct here |
|---|---|---|
| README | a newcomer scanning | leads with the point; second person; imperative |
| Design doc / RFC / ADR | a peer deciding | prose earns its length; the argument must follow |
| Test plan / test case | a tester executing | imperative, precise; quality adjectives are findings |
| QA report | someone making a release call | verdict first with its condition; counts, not adjectives |
| Bug report | whoever reproduces it | the reproducer is the document; verbatim error text |
| API / CLI reference | someone looking one thing up | consistency beats flow; every example runs |
| Release notes | someone asking "does this affect me" | changes first, terse |
| Slide content | read in three seconds while someone talks | fragments right, sentences wrong |
| Talk track / demo script | **listened to** | contractions right, long clauses wrong, punctuation invisible |

Four kinds have their own criteria, including per-kind review checklists. Read the matching
file before judging:

| Reviewing | Read |
|---|---|
| Design doc, RFC, ADR, proposal | [reference/design-docs.md](reference/design-docs.md) |
| README, contributing guide, project docs | [reference/readmes.md](reference/readmes.md) |
| Test plan, test case, QA report, bug report | [reference/test-plans.md](reference/test-plans.md) |
| API reference, CLI docs, tool docs, schema docs | [reference/api-reference.md](reference/api-reference.md) |

## 2. Run the script

    ./check-prose.sh <file>

It locates the mechanical tells: the symbol set (em dash, en dash, spaced hyphen, curly
quotes, ellipsis, arrows, emoji), the em-dash rate per thousand words, and the term tables
for inflated vocabulary, filler, openers, contrast frames, hedges, unobservable quality
words and relative time.

**A hit is a located candidate, not a finding.** The script does the searching, which a
model does unreliably on its own writing, and leaves the ruling to step 3. It exits 0 with
hits for exactly that reason. Hedging where a fact is genuinely uncertain is the word doing
its job.

**Run it, do not reimplement it.** Judging your own register is the one thing a generator
is worst at, because fluent-and-empty is its own baseline.

### What the script cannot reach

Named so a clean run is never read as a clean document:

- **The full contrast frame.** It catches `not just` and `not only`; the shape
  "it isn't A, it's B" has open slots and needs a reader.
- **Rule of three.** Matched triads carrying one idea have no fixed words.
- **Restatement.** The next sentence saying the last one again.
- **Vagueness.** A claim with no number, name or path in it, that no pattern marks.
- **Uniform sentence length**, and prose chopped into bullets.
- **Whether a hedge is earned**, which is the whole judgment.

## 3. Judge

**Lead with the highest level.** Structural problems make sentence edits wasted work, so
settle them first:

1. **Does it serve its purpose?** Wrong reader, missing decision, a document that should
   not exist.
2. **Is the structure right?** Missing sections, wrong order, buried conclusion.
3. **Is it accurate?** Broken examples, stale versions, unsupported claims.
4. **Is the prose clean?** Voice, terminology, hedging.

**Front-load.** Readers stop early. The conclusion, the recommendation, or the working
command belongs on the first screen. This applies fractally: the first sentence of every
section states its point.

**The sentence rules**, each a finding when broken:

- Present tense, active voice. "The validator rejects the field", not "the field will be
  rejected".
- Imperative for instructions. "Run the migration", not "you should run the migration".
- One term per concept, forever. Choosing `test case` means never writing `test`, `case` or
  `TC` for it. Synonym variation is a virtue in prose and a defect in technical writing:
  the reader has to decide whether a new word means a new thing.
- Quantify. "Slow" becomes "roughly 4s per 1000 records"; "large" becomes "over 50 MB".
- No dangling pronouns. "This causes failures" — this what? Name the referent.
- Split a sentence carrying more than one clause of new information. Three commas is
  usually three sentences.
- Second person for the reader's actions, not first person plural.
- No relative time. "Currently", "recently", "the new API" rot on their own. Write the
  condition: "in v2.3 and later".

**Cut 20%.** Not rhetorical. First drafts run reliably long, and the cut almost always
improves them.

**Give the reasoning with the correction.** "Moved the recommendation up, because a
reviewer approving this will not read past the first screen" teaches; a silent reordering
does not.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Kind, reader and register established
    - [ ] Matching reference/ file read, if one applies
    - [ ] check-prose.sh run, output kept
    - [ ] Each hit ruled on — cost the reader, or not
    - [ ] The shapes the script cannot reach, judged by reading
    - [ ] Verdict reported

1. **Identify** (step 1). If the kind is genuinely unclear, ask rather than guess.
2. **Run the script** (step 2).
3. **Judge** (step 3), highest level first, whole document.
4. **Report** (below).
5. **Fix, if asked.** The smallest change that lands the words, in the author's voice.
   Leave what already works.

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    REVISE — reads as a design doc but the recommendation is on screen three.
    Next: move the recommendation up, then re-run the script.
    Run it, or see the findings?

- **PASS** — fits its reader, leads with the point, says the true thing.
- **REVISE** — findings, each quoting the words at fault and naming the smallest fix.

Findings, the script output, and the trace are prepared and held until asked. When findings
are given, quote the text rather than describing it, and say which came from the script and
which from reading: a count is reproducible and a judgment is not, and the reader is
entitled to know which they are being handed.

## How I used issue 20

**Taken nearly whole:**

- **The Symbol table** → the `sym` block: em dash, en dash, spaced hyphen, ellipsis, curly quotes and apostrophe, bullet character, arrow, exclamation, emoji.
- **The Term tables** → the `term` block, keeping your four groupings — inflated vocabulary, filler, openers and transitions, contrast frames — plus the QA-specific set, where `verify that` / `properly` / `correctly` / `as expected` became the "unobservable" check.

**Dropped deliberately: spaced colon and spaced semicolon.** Your own analysis argues against them — the colon tell is a layout shape that a spaced `:` catches almost none of, and the 2026 measurements run the other way on semicolons, so a rule there penalises the human habit. I followed the reasoning rather than the table.

**Changed: em-dash rate is now measured.** Issue 20 lists "em dashes per 1,000 words" under what the engine cannot express, since a Rule fires per occurrence and nothing counts. A shell script can count, so the rate is in. It immediately caught 15 per 1000 in a file I wrote yesterday.

**Not taken:** the delivery question — SQL file versus server seeding versus README. That is testcase-validator's architecture and its ADR-0006 constraint, not ours.

inflated vocabulary, filler, openers, contrast frames, hedges,
unobservable quality words and relative time. It exits 0 with hits on
purpose: a hit is a located candidate, and only judgment rules on it.

What the script cannot reach is named in the skill so a clean run is never
read as a clean document: the open-slot contrast frame, rule of three,
restatement, vagueness, uniform sentence length, and whether a hedge is
earned.

Step 3 leads with the highest level, since structural problems make
sentence edits wasted work, and carries the sentence rules: present tense
and active voice, imperative for instructions, one term per concept,
quantify, no dangling pronouns, no relative time, cut 20%.

checklists — design docs, READMEs, test plans and QA reports, API
reference. Each is read on demand rather than loaded up front.

The emoji check probes for grep -P rather than assuming it. On BSD and
macOS the flag is absent, and a suppressed error there would report no
emoji on a file full of them, which is worse than not checking at all.

input.prompt: Summarize this discussion: what is being proposed for saving per-repo agent history through agent traces? What is the file format, where do traces get stored, what problem does it solve, and what is the current status or maintainer response?

content.content:
# Summary of GitHub Discussion #45334

## Proposal
The discussion proposes enabling Zed to persistently save agent conversation history in a standardized, repository-integrated format rather than requiring manual exports.

## Storage & Format
The original proposal suggested storing traces in `.zed/agent-history/` within projects, configured via `.zed/settings.json`. However, the author evolved the idea toward adopting the "agent trace" standard developed by Cursor, which would use JSON serialization to preserve complete conversation data including context, agent selection, and thinking processes—addressing limitations of lossy Markdown exports.

## Problems Addressed
- Agent history currently disappears between sessions across all projects
- Manual Markdown exports lack crucial metadata (selected context, file state at inclusion time, model selection, reasoning steps)
- Users cannot reopen exported conversations with full fidelity
- No collaborative capability between team members continuing shared agent threads

## Current Status
**No maintainer response is evident in this excerpt.** The discussion remains open with 5 comments. A related issue (#8325) was referenced indicating Zed lacks necessary integration hooks that competitors like Claude Code and Copilot CLI already provide. The author suggested Zed could integrate with third-party tools (git-ai, blameprompt) that already support the agent trace specification.

# Redesign draft — session-log workflow on GitHub/GitLab

**Status: draft for discussion. Nothing here is applied. No current file is touched.**

Written 2026-08-16 from the requests below. The skills named in section 4 do not exist yet.

---

## 1. What you asked for, this turn

| # | Request | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Stop using story files | `docs/stories/` is already deleted. Nothing in the toolkit writes or reads a story now, so this is a decision to record rather than work to do |
| 2 | Mimic Zed's session-log export | A session is written to the repo so a later agent can read what actually happened |
| 3 | Save the session **raw** — no cutting, no summarising, no extraction | Drift comes from the gap between what was decided and what was written down. Summarising is where that gap opens |
| 4 | Redesign the workflow around it | The units below |
| 4a | Use the platform as far as it goes | Issues, labels, PRs, dependencies are the state. The toolkit stops holding state of its own |
| 4b | One skill per lifecycle step | create issue · create task · solve issue · do task · review · create PR · merge |
| 4c | Skills trigger on the **action** the user asks for | "file an issue" reaches create-issue, which attaches the session log without being told |
| 4d | Each skill gets a template and steps carrying enough context | The template is what stops a thin issue reaching an agent |
| 5 | Draft this in a temp folder | This file |
| 6 | Touch nothing yet | Nothing touched |

## 2. What Zed is actually doing, and what it says about the idea

From the open Zed discussion on per-repo agent history (#45334), and the agent-panel docs:

| Fact | Bearing on this design |
|---|---|
| Threads are exportable as Markdown today, by hand | Manual export is the state of the art, and it is not enough |
| The proposal is to store history per repo, under a project directory, configured in project settings | Same shape as writing to `.sessions/` here |
| The author moved from "save markdown" to adopting an **agent trace** standard, JSON, because markdown export is **lossy** | The strongest support for your point 3 |
| What markdown loses: the context that was selected, **the file state at the time it was included**, model selection, reasoning steps | This is the drift you are describing, named by someone else independently |
| Nobody can reopen an exported conversation at full fidelity | A session log is a record, not a resumable state — worth being honest about |
| Open discussion, no maintainer response, blocked on integration hooks Zed lacks | The standard is not settled. Do not bind to `agent-trace` yet |

**The useful conclusion:** the idea is validated, the format is not. Write raw markdown transcripts now, keep the door open to a trace format later.

## 3. The mechanism

```
   a session happens
        │
        ▼
   .sessions/<date>-<slug>.md        raw, whole, unedited

---
name: file-issue
description: |
  Turns something said in a session into a tracked issue that a cold agent can act on,
  and saves the raw session beside it as the context the issue body cannot carry. Decides
  first whether the thing needs tracking at all, searches for an existing issue before
  creating a second one, quotes the request in the words it was made in rather than
  paraphrasing it, and states an acceptance test someone else can check. Creates the
  portal every later step resolves back to.
when_to_use: |
  Use whenever work is identified but not started — "this is broken", "we should track
  this", "file an issue", "raise a bug", "that's a separate problem", "let's do that
  later", "add it to the backlog", "someone should fix that". Reach for it when a session
  surfaces a second problem while working on a first, which is the case that most often
  goes unrecorded. Do not reach for it for a question, a thing already being done, or a
  fix smaller than the issue describing it.
argument-hint: "[what to file]"
---

# File an issue

Target: $ARGUMENTS — what to file, or the thing just discussed.

**The issue is a portal, not a record.** Everything after it resolves backwards through
it: a branch takes its name, a commit cites it, a PR closes it, and an agent picking up
cold reads it first. What it cannot do is carry the reasoning that produced it — an issue
body is a summary by nature, and summarising is where the intent shifts.

So the split is: **the issue states the decision and the test; the session log holds the
reasoning.** The issue links to the log rather than absorbing it.

## 1. Should this be an issue at all

The judgment the whole workflow rests on. File too eagerly and the tracker fills with
things nobody closes; too reluctantly and the work happens with no record.

**Do not file:**

- A question the reply answers.
- A fix smaller than the issue describing it. A typo takes ten seconds; the issue takes
  two minutes and a close.
- Thinking aloud, exploring an idea, weighing an approach. A decision is not yet made.
- Something already being done in this session and about to be committed.

**Do file:**

- A second problem surfaced while working on a first. **This is the case that goes
  unrecorded most often** — the session ends and the observation dies with it.
- Anything that will be picked up by someone, or something, other than this session.
- A decision made here that later work must not silently reverse.

**Uncertain? Ask.** A user who says "we should probably…" has not decided. One question is
cheaper than an issue nobody wanted.

## 2. Search before creating

    gh issue list --search "<key terms>" --state all --limit 20

A second issue for the same thing splits its history, and nothing says which one is live.
On a hit, comment on the existing issue instead and say that is what you did.

## 3. Save the session

Write the raw session to `.sessions/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` and commit it.

**Raw. Whole. Unedited.** No summary, no "key decisions" section, no extraction. The
moment anyone decides what mattered, the thing that mattered and was not obvious is gone.
That is the drift this whole design exists to remove, and it is undone by one helpful edit.

Append a generated heading index at the top — headings only, no prose — so a later reader
can find a section without reading to it. Generating an index is not summarising: it adds
no judgment and removes nothing.

## 4. Write the issue

    ## What
    <the ask, quoted in the words it was made in>

    ## Why
    <the problem behind it — what breaks, or costs, if this is not done>

    ## Done when
    - [ ] <observable, checkable by someone who was not here>

    ## Context
    Session: .sessions/2026-08-16-<slug>.md
    <the part worth reading, by heading or line range>

    ## Out of scope
    <what this deliberately does not cover>

**Quote, do not paraphrase.** "The report reads as a wall when it lands in Slack" is what
was said. "Improve report formatting" is what an agent does with it, and the two are not
the same instruction. Paraphrase is the first place intent shifts, and it happens before
anyone can notice.

**"Done when" is the whole issue.** An acceptance line a third party can check is what
makes this pickable cold. *"No open Sev-1 defects and 95% of planned cases executed"* is
checkable; *"quality is acceptable"* is not. If you cannot write one, the thing is not
ready to be an issue and the honest move is to say so.

**"Out of scope" is load-bearing.** It records a decision, so a later gap reads as a known
tradeoff rather than an oversight — and it is what stops the next agent widening the work.

**Link, never inline.** Pasting the session into the issue body is the summarising failure
by another route: it makes the issue unreadable and the log redundant at once.

## 5. Create it, and say where it went

    gh issue create --title "<one line, states the problem not the fix>" --body-file <file>

Then declare the platform state the issue starts in: whatever label marks *ready to be
picked up* in this project. Where the project declares none, say so rather than inventing
one.

Blocked by something? Record it as a real dependency, not a sentence in the body — the
platform can answer "what is unblocked" and prose cannot.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Decided it needs tracking — and said why, if it was close
    - [ ] Searched for an existing issue
    - [ ] Session saved raw to .sessions/, committed
    - [ ] Body written: what (quoted), why, done-when, context, out of scope
    - [ ] Issue created, labelled, dependencies recorded
    - [ ] Verdict reported

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    FILED — #42, blocked by #38, session at .sessions/2026-08-16-report-wall.md
    Next: nothing. It is pickable when #38 closes.
    Want the body?

When it was decided *not* to file, that is still a verdict and still needs saying:

    NOT FILED — a typo fix, already done in this session.
    Next: nothing.

The body, the search results and the session path are prepared and held until asked.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive overview of GitHub issue template structure and best practices:

## GitHub Issue Template Structure Best Practices

### Basic Issue Template Components

Issue templates are pre-filled forms that contributors pick when they create an issue (bug, feature request, docs, etc.). GitHub allows you to configure these templates in the .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE folder of your repository.

### Recommended Template Structure

For bug reports, a typical structure includes:
- Description, Steps to Reproduce, Expected Behavior, Actual Behavior, Environment (OS, Browser/Version), and Additional Information (screenshots, logs, or other helpful details)

### Key Best Practices

Searched both halves. Evaluation below.

## `bug.md`

| Field | Best practice | We have | Worth adding? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Title states the symptom | universal | in `SKILL.md` §5, not the template | **Yes** — one line, and it's the field most often wrong |
| Steps to reproduce | universal, "the" required field | ✅ `## Reproduce` | — |
| Expected vs actual | universal | ✅ both, actual verbatim | — |
| Frequency / reproducibility | named repeatedly | ✅ `always \| N of M` | — |
| **Severity** — technical impact | universal | ❌ | **No** — a label, not a body section. Platform-native, filterable |
| **Priority** — business urgency | called out as *distinct* from severity | ❌ | **No**, same reason. But worth saying they're two things, since one field collapses both |
| **Environment** — OS, version, build, device | universal, own section | ⚠️ one clause inside Reproduce | **Yes** — promote it. "Passes on one firmware, fails on another" is underspecification, not flakiness |
| Screenshot / recording / attachment | universal | ❌ | **Weak yes** — one line. Cheap, and the reproducer is the document |
| Console errors / logs | common | ⚠️ "log excerpt" inside Actual | No — already covered |
| Reporter + date | common | ❌ | **No** — the platform supplies author and timestamp. Adding it duplicates state |
| **Root cause** | ❌ rare in generic templates | ✅ + "say what was ruled out" | — *your requirement, and stronger than the standard* |
| **Proposed fix** | ❌ rare | ✅ + what it doesn't fix | — *same* |
| **Out of scope** | ❌ rare | ✅ | — *rare and genuinely load-bearing* |
| **Session link** | ❌ absent everywhere | ✅ | — *the whole design* |

## `task.md`

| Field | Best practice | We have | Worth adding? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Acceptance criteria, pass/fail, per-item | universal; markdown checklist | ✅ `## Done when` | — |
| **Definition of Done** — project-wide, stable, separate from AC | explicitly distinguished from AC | ❌ conflated into `Done when` | **Yes, but not here** — DoD is one project-level list, not a per-issue section. Belongs in the profile or a repo doc |
| Plan / steps | common | ✅ with per-step verify | — |
| Expected outcome | less common | ✅ stated as end-state, not work | — |
| What's next / successor | rare | ✅ | — |
| Estimate, milestone, labels | common | ❌ | **No** — platform fields, not body sections |
| User story format ("As a… I want…") | common in agile templates | ❌ | **No** — you just deleted stories. Reintroducing the form would contradict that |

## The one finding that isn't a field

**Research says five or six required fields maximum — too much detail discourages contributions.** `bug.md` has eight sections and `task.md` has eight. That's a real tension, and it resolves differently for you than for a generic project: these are filled by an agent that has the session in front of it, not by a drive-by reporter. The cost of a long template lands on a human filing by hand through the web form.

If you want one mitigation, it's marking which sections are required and which are optional, so a human can skip four of them and an agent still fills all eight.

**My recommendation: add three.** Title guidance and Environment to `bug.md` (both genuinely missing), and a required/optional marking on both. Skip severity, priority, estimate and reporter — all four are platform fields, and putting them in the body is the thing your 4a is against.

Two things I put in the comments while there, both from the research and both cheap: severity and priority are labels rather than sections, and they're two different things that one field collapses; and `Done when` is this task's acceptance criteria, not the project's definition of done, which belongs in one project-level document instead of being restated in every issue.

Target: $ARGUMENTS — what to file, or the thing just discussed.

body is a summary by nature, and summarising is where the intent shifts.

reasoning.** The issue links to the log rather than absorbing it.

| label | `gh issue edit --add-label` | `glab issue update --label` |
| change request | `pr` | `mr` |
| templates live in | `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` | `.gitlab/issue_templates/`, reachable as `--template <name>` |

inside the clone.

natively. GitLab's blocking relationships are a paid tier; on a free instance the reachable
verb is `--linked-issues` with `--link-type relates_to`, which records a relation but does
not gate anything. Say which you got — a relation reported as a dependency is a promise the
platform will not keep.

## 1. Should this be an issue at all

The judgment the whole workflow rests on. File too eagerly and the tracker fills with
things nobody closes; too reluctantly and the work happens with no record.

**Do not file:**

- A question the reply answers.
- A fix smaller than the issue describing it. A typo takes ten seconds; the issue takes
  two minutes and a close.
- Thinking aloud, exploring an idea, weighing an approach. A decision is not yet made.
- Something already being done in this session and about to be committed.

**Do file:**

- A second problem surfaced while working on a first. **This is the case that goes
  unrecorded most often** — the session ends and the observation dies with it.
- Anything that will be picked up by someone, or something, other than this session.
- A decision made here that later work must not silently reverse.

**Uncertain? Ask.** A user who says "we should probably…" has not decided. One question is
cheaper than an issue nobody wanted.

    glab issue list --search "<key terms>" --in title,description --all

can find a section without reading to it. Generating an index is not summarising: it adds
no judgment and removes nothing.

The body skeleton is not in this file. It ships as a template, so that a person filing
through the web interface gets the same sections an agent does:

| The thing is | Template | The sections it exists for |
|---|---|---|
| something broken | [templates/bug.md](templates/bug.md) | **Root cause** and **Proposed fix** — a bug without either is a report, not an issue |

kind that needs a section neither template has gets it, and the template gains it
afterwards.

**Place them where the platform looks**, so the CLI and the web form agree:
`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` or `.gitlab/issue_templates/`. On GitLab the flag reads them
directly: `glab issue create --template bug`.

ready to be an issue, and the honest move is to say so rather than file it anyway.

**Link, never inline.** Pasting the session into the body is the summarising failure by

## 5. Create it, and say where it went

    gh   issue create --title "<states the problem, not the fix>" --body-file <f>
    glab issue create --title "<states the problem, not the fix>" -d "$(cat <f>)"

    - [ ] Decided it needs tracking — and said why, if it was close
